pages.title: Foundations: Unbounded vs Bounded Data
bulletPoints: Streaming data is inherently unbounded: An infinite, continuously arriving stream of real-time events.
Batch processing is simply a subset of stream processing where the stream is artificially bounded at a point in time.
Historical batch pipelines introduced hours of latency; streaming provides instantaneous insights and fast reaction.
Key architectural challenge: Processing unbounded streams accurately despite out-of-order and delayed arrivals.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Batch = Stream bounded at time T

pages.title: Batch vs Streaming: Evolution of Data Architectures
bulletPoints: Lambda Architecture: Running dual systems—a fast streaming layer (Storm) and an accurate batch layer (Hadoop/MapReduce).
Flaws of Lambda: Maintaining two separate codebases, dual business logic, and reconciling discrepancies between them.
Kappa Architecture: A single unified stream processing engine (Flink/Beam) that processes both real-time and historical data.
Unified API: The same transform code processes streaming events and re-processes historical logs from storage.

pages.title: Event Time vs Processing Time: The Critical Distinction
bulletPoints: Event Time: The exact timestamp when an event originally occurred on the client device or sensor.
Processing Time: The timestamp when the stream processing engine receives and executes the event.
Ingestion Time: The timestamp when the event is appended to the message broker (e.g. Kafka partition).
The Golden Rule: For correct business calculations, grouping and windowing must always be based on Event Time.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Event Time != Processing Time != Ingestion Time

pages.title: Skew and Watermarks: Measuring Event Time Progress
bulletPoints: Event-time skew: The delay between event time and processing time caused by network latency and client offline periods.
A Watermark is a monotonically increasing timestamp representing system progress: "All data up to time T has arrived".
Heuristic vs Perfect watermarks: Heuristic watermarks estimate arrival completeness based on observed network delays.
Watermark propagation: In a multi-stage streaming pipeline, the watermark is the minimum watermark of all input channels.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Watermark(T) => All events with event_time < T have arrived

pages.title: The Four Core Questions of Stream Processing
bulletPoints: What is being computed? Defined by the transformation logic (e.g., Sum, Count, Average, Machine Learning inference).
Where in event time is it computed? Defined by the windowing strategy (Tumbling, Sliding, or Session windows).
When in processing time are results materialized? Governed by triggers and watermark progression.
How do those results relate? Governed by the accumulation mode (Discarding, Accumulating, or Retracting).

pages.title: Windowing Strategies: Fixed (Tumbling) Windows
bulletPoints: Fixed windows segment time into non-overlapping, contiguous intervals of uniform duration (e.g. 5-minute windows).
Every event belongs to exactly one fixed window based on its event time.
Window boundaries: Window [12:00, 12:05) contains all events with timestamps 12:00:00 <= t < 12:05:00.
Common use cases: Hourly revenue aggregates, 10-minute sensor telemetry summaries, and daily active user metrics.

pages.title: Sliding (Hopping) Windows & Multi-Bucket Aggregation
bulletPoints: Sliding windows have a fixed length and a slide period (e.g., 1-hour window sliding every 5 minutes).
Overlap factor: Since the window duration exceeds the slide period, events belong to multiple overlapping windows.
Efficient execution: Stream processors maintain micro-aggregates for the slide period to avoid redundant calculations.
Common use cases: Moving averages, stock trading volume trends, and sliding 15-minute anomaly detection.

pages.title: Session Windows: Dynamic Inactivity Gaps
bulletPoints: Session windows are data-driven windows defined by periods of user activity separated by an inactivity gap (e.g. 30 mins).
No fixed size: A session can last 2 minutes or 5 hours depending on how long the user remains active.
Dynamic window merging: As out-of-order events arrive, two previously disjoint session windows may merge into one.
Ideal for web analytics: Tracking e-commerce user browsing journeys and game play sessions.

pages.title: Watermarks & Completeness: Handling Late Data
bulletPoints: No matter how well-tuned a watermark is, mobile devices reconnecting after hours offline produce late data.
Allowed lateness: Configurable horizon specifying how long window state is preserved after the watermark passes.
Once allowed lateness expires, the window is permanently closed, and any subsequent events are routed to a dead-letter queue.
Trade-off: Longer allowed lateness ensures higher accuracy but requires keeping state in memory longer.

pages.title: Triggers: Controlling When Results Materialize
bulletPoints: Triggers dictate the exact instant in processing time when intermediate or final window results are emitted.
Watermark triggers: Fire when the watermark sweeps past the end of the window (standard completeness trigger).
Processing-time triggers: Fire periodically (e.g. every 10 seconds) to emit speculative previews before window close.
Data-driven triggers: Fire every N elements (e.g. emit every 1,000 events) for high-frequency dashboards.

pages.title: Speculative Triggers & Punctual Updates
bulletPoints: Low latency vs high accuracy: Users need low-latency estimates immediately, but also want final accurate values later.
Composite triggers: Fire a speculative estimate every 5 seconds until the watermark arrives, then fire late updates if needed.
Eliminating stale caches: Downstream dashboards can update progress bars in real time without waiting for full batch completion.
Graceful refinement: The system converges monotonically on the exact answer as data arrives.

pages.title: Accumulation Modes: Discarding, Accumulating & Retracting
bulletPoints: Discarding: Each firing emits only the delta (new events) since the last trigger firing; past state is discarded.
Accumulating: Each firing emits the full updated aggregate (e.g. running total 10 -> 15 -> 22); downstream overwrites.
Retracting: Emits both a retraction of the previous estimate (-15) and the new value (+22) for downstream aggregators.
Retraction pipelines: Essential when feeding downstream relational tables that perform secondary groupings.

pages.title: Exactly-Once Processing Semantics (EOS)
bulletPoints: At-least-once: Events are guaranteed to be processed, but network retries may duplicate records (over-counting).
At-most-once: Events are dropped under failure; no duplicates, but data loss occurs.
Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS): Every record impacts the final computed output state exactly once, despite failures.
Implementation: Requires end-to-end integration across replayable sources (Kafka), stateful engines, and transactional sinks.
pages.formulaOrSummary: At-Least-Once + Idempotent / Two-Phase Commit Sink = Exactly-Once

pages.title: State Management in Stream Processors
bulletPoints: Stateful streaming: Operations like aggregations, joins, and sessionization require persistent state between events.
Embedded state backends: Embedded key-value stores (e.g. RocksDB) store state locally on disk with in-memory caching.
Scalability: Local embedded state eliminates remote database RPC overheads, enabling millions of operations per second.
State pruning: State must be tied to TTLs or window lifetimes to prevent unbounded disk growth over months.

pages.title: Checkpointing & Distributed Snapshots (Chandy-Lamport)
bulletPoints: Asynchronous barrier snapshotting: Checkpoint barriers flow alongside data records through operator DAGs.
When an operator receives a barrier from all inputs, it snapshots its local state to durable storage (S3/HDFS).
Non-blocking: Stream processing continues without pausing while state is uploaded asynchronously in the background.
Recovery: On worker crash, the entire pipeline rolls back to the last completed checkpoint and replays stream sources.

pages.title: Stream Joins: Windowed Stream-to-Stream Joins
bulletPoints: Joining two unbounded streams (e.g., ad impressions and ad clicks) requires a bounding window in event time.
Interval join: Join event A with event B where event_time_B is within [event_time_A - 10m, event_time_A + 30m].
State retention: Both streams buffer events in state until the join condition is satisfied or the interval window expires.
Clean-up: Expired unjoined records can be emitted as outer joins (e.g., impressions that never received a click).

pages.title: The Stream-Table Duality
bulletPoints: A stream is a changelog of events over time; a table is the materialized snapshot of state at a single point in time.
Stream -> Table: Aggregating a changelog of inserts, updates, and deletes produces a current state table.
Table -> Stream: Capturing the change-data-capture (CDC) log of a database table produces an event stream.
Unifying paradigm: Streams and tables are two sides of the same coin, formalized in Kafka Streams (KStream/KTable) and Flink.

pages.title: Temporal Joins & Dimension Table Lookups
bulletPoints: Joining an event stream with an evolving dimension table (e.g. transaction stream joined with customer credit score table).
Temporal tables preserve historical versioning: Query the customer’s credit score *at the exact time of the transaction*.
Eliminates race conditions: Changes to customer profile today do not retroactively invalidate transactions from yesterday.
Native support in SQL streaming engines via versioned state snapshots and changelog joins.

pages.title: Handling Out-of-Order Data: DLQs & Late Routing
bulletPoints: Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ): Route unparseable, malformed, or hopelessly late events to a dedicated isolation topic.
Automated alerts: Monitor DLQ volume to detect client app regressions, corrupted schema encoders, or protocol mismatches.
Offline re-drive: Once bugs in processing logic are resolved, messages from the DLQ can be replayed and re-injected safely.
Zero data loss: Isolating bad records prevents toxic payloads from blocking processing threads.

pages.title: Backpressure: Downstream Flow Control
bulletPoints: When downstream operators cannot keep up with upstream arrival rates, buffers fill up rapidly.
Reactive backpressure: Slow downstream operators stop pulling from input buffers, propagating backpressure upstream.
TCP flow control: Buffers fill up to network sockets, ultimately signaling the message broker consumer to slow down.
Graceful throttling: The cluster slows down gracefully instead of crashing due to out-of-memory errors.

pages.title: Dynamic Autoscaling in Streaming Topologies
bulletPoints: Streaming workloads experience diurnal traffic peaks (e.g. evening shopping spikes, weekend sports events).
Autoscaling triggers: Scale workers based on consumer group lag and operator CPU utilization.
State redistribution: When adding new workers, stream state partitions must rebalance across the expanded worker pool.
Reactive vs predictive scaling: Use predictive historical models to scale up clusters 15 minutes before anticipated peaks.

pages.title: Streaming SQL: Declarative Relational Processing
bulletPoints: Standard SQL syntax extended with streaming primitives: TUMBLE(ts, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE), HOP, and SESSION.
Apache Calcite and Flink SQL translate declarative queries into optimized stateful physical operator graphs.
Democratization: Data analysts and engineers query real-time streams using familiar SELECT, WHERE, and GROUP BY.
Continuous queries: A streaming SQL query runs continuously, producing an output changelog stream.

pages.title: Operator Chaining & Memory Management
bulletPoints: Operator chaining: Fuses adjacent operators (e.g., filter -> map) into a single thread to eliminate serialization overhead.
Off-heap memory management: Allocate state and network buffers outside JVM garbage collection to eliminate GC pauses.
Zero-copy network transfers: Pass memory segments directly between Netty network channels and operator buffers.
Sub-millisecond latency: Chaining and off-heap memory achieve consistent microsecond-to-millisecond end-to-end latencies.

pages.title: Monitoring & Operating Streaming Topologies
bulletPoints: Key streaming metrics: Source ingestion lag, event-time watermark latency, checkpoint duration, and GC pause times.
Watermark lag: The difference between current wall-clock time and the pipeline watermark reveals if data processing is falling behind.
Checkpoint size growth: Track state size to identify leaking keys or unbounded state accumulators.
Alerting: Alert when checkpoint duration exceeds checkpoint interval, which indicates imminent cluster stalling.

pages.title: The Future of Streaming: Unified Real-Time Platforms
bulletPoints: Convergence of streaming and storage: Modern lakehouse architectures (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake) ingest streaming updates directly.
Serverless streaming: Instant spin-up of compute operators without managing dedicated distributed clusters.
Real-time AI/ML feature stores: Continuous stream processors compute live features for online fraud detection and recommendation.
Streaming as default: All future data architectures will treat batch as a historical subset of continuous event streaming.
